statement: This session (week 1, day 2) continues with the remaining four fragments of the course framework: scaling, concurrency, delegation and communication, all discussed in the context of Medium with a focus on nitty-gritty implementation details and performance benefits.
case_study: Medium is the running case study for all four fragments.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: today we'll continue our discussion on the other four properties, other four fragments of it. Scaling, concurrency, delegation, and communication.

statement: The teacher does not provide transcripts of recorded lectures: it is a one-person effort, and a GitHub transcription tool he tried misinterpreted the class's accent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When one person team, I cannot transcribe

statement: No post-lecture read-ups are given: about 90% of people do not even read the pre-reads, and the lecture flow is not fixed; it changes cohort to cohort and is biased towards what the teacher has learned recently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I typically don't give post lecture read-ups because 90% folks don't even read pre-reads.

statement: Whenever you hear a term or find something interesting in the lecture, Google it, read and explore it yourself rather than relying on a curated link list; the internet evolves, curated links go stale, and exploring primary sources (e.g. MySQL's documentation on how it implements datetime) leads to serendipitous, more interesting findings and makes you a better engineer.
detail: Teacher believes in serendipity: you look for one thing and land on something 1000x more interesting. Only pre-reads are given, to prepare for a lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whatever I utter, just Google, find and read and explore, as simple as that.

statement: There are no participant introductions in class: with about 80 participants at one minute each it would take ~80 minutes (in the first cohort, 25 people took almost 40 minutes); participants can connect over Discord instead. The course is 8 weeks / 16 sessions and kept crisp and focused on engineering.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 80 folks participation itself or introduction itself would take an hour.

statement: Students are encouraged to keep giving feedback on what to improve or cover; the teacher will act on it where there is scope.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: feel free to add to context feedback how I can improve, what all things I can cover.

statement: Today's agenda in order: caching at different levels, scaling, delegation, concurrency, communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the first thing that we'll discuss today is caching at different levels.

statement: Concurrency gets only 5-10 minutes today; week 2, day 1 covers concurrency in depth (how database concurrency falls apart) using practical examples.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Concurrency will spend like 5-10 minutes because next week, first day, like second week, first day, we have an in-depth coverage of concurrency.

statement: Concurrency is the heart and soul of building systems at scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because that is the heart and soul of building systems at scale.

statement: Today's delegation section covers the basics you definitely need to know.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But delegation will cover basics that you definitely need to know.

statement: Caching at different levels means asking, for every place in the architecture: what would you cache there, where exactly does the cache sit, and what benefit (saved computation or I/O) do you get.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What you're caching, where you're caching, what benefits are you getting out of?

statement: A student framed caching at multiple layers vaguely as 'reducing latency'; the teacher pushed for a concrete answer about where in the architecture the cache sits, saying you cannot just have one centralized cache and need to be more creative about placement.
detail: Student 6: caching at multiple layers reduces latency (response speed inversely proportional to latency). Correction: name the exact place in the architecture and the benefit.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you cannot just have one centralized cache where you are storing things, that you need to come up more creative

statement: Don't think of a cache only as a centralized remote cache, which is what comes to mind most naturally; look for other places that can act as a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we always think of cache as centralized [?remote] cache... But apart from this, there are other places can use as a cache.

statement: An application-level cache can be just a hash map in the main memory (RAM) of the API server, used alongside a centralized remote cache such as Redis that sits in front of the database.
detail: Proposed by Student 3 and confirmed by the teacher, who drew users -> API servers -> database with a remote cache (Redis) and an in-memory cache on the API server.
case_study: Medium API servers can keep frequently read data in RAM in addition to the central Redis.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you can use the RAM of your machine, RAM of your API server to cache things.

statement: Disadvantages of an in-memory cache on the API server: its size is limited by the memory the application needs; the cache is lost if the application goes down or crashes; and with multiple instances each instance has a different cache, causing inconsistency.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if you're distributing this application at some level, all the different instances will have different caches.

statement: Inconsistency arises because keeping each instance's local cache fresh is hard: one instance may get a hot entry refreshed often while another instance lags behind, so some users see an inconsistent view.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the second instance starts lagging behind or does not get enough updates

statement: A centralized cache (e.g. a separate Redis instance contacted by all application instances) avoids this inconsistency because it is a single source of truth, but then you give up the local in-memory cache.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because it is a single source of truth. Yeah. So then you cannot have this.

statement: The API server's main memory is local to that server and not accessible from anywhere else. Since there are multiple API servers, data cached on one server is not seen by the others; if the next request goes to another server it misses, makes the DB call, populates its own cache and returns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you're using the main memory of API server, it is local to this particular server.

statement: The reason to cache in the API server's memory is not consistency but performance: it saves an expensive network call to the remote cache. The teacher calls it an extremely interesting hack that gives a massive performance boost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What you are saving is an expensive network call to the cache by caching the same data over here.

statement: With sticky sessions (the load balancer always sends a given user's requests to the same server), you can cache that user's data in that server's main memory, since the user's requests never go to another server; a centralized remote cache can still exist alongside.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in case you have sticky sessions, let's say request of a particular user will always go to a particular server always

statement: Caching in API server memory gives up strong consistency between the caches; whether that is acceptable is use-case specific.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But here you're giving up on strong consistency between cache and it should be okay. It's use case specific.

statement: Using API server memory as a cache is underappreciated; many startups use it as a hack for performance, while big companies typically don't.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a lot of startups use it as hack. Big companies typically don't

statement: Local API-server caching works when the data is nearly static and you don't need immediate updates, i.e. serving stale data to some users for a while is fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this also works where your data is nearly static.

statement: Published blogs (LinkedIn blogs, Medium blogs) are nearly static: once published a blog is very unlikely to change, and database updates for a published item are very infrequent. So even if two different copies are cached on different API servers, that is fine, and Medium can use API server memory as a cache for them.
case_study: Cache published Medium blogs in API server main memory; staleness across servers is acceptable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: blog once published, very unlikely that it would be changed again.

statement: Caching is not either/or: systems usually have multi-level caches, e.g. a local in-memory cache on the API server along with the centralized remote cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm not saying it's either this or this, right? Always we [?often], have multi-level caches.

statement: Caching some (not all) information locally, with an expiry, saves the network I/O to the remote cache and reduces load on the Redis server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This network I.O. you are reducing, the load on this Redis server, by caching the same information on local machine, not all, some information ...

statement: Because an API server has very limited RAM, TTLs on the local cache and the flushing strategy are very important.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this API server, it has very limited RAM, so having TTL is very important. How you flush the cache is very important.

statement: One option is to run a local Redis on the API server itself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can run a local Redis on this server itself, a lot of fancy stuff

statement: A student proposed database views as a form of caching: they save executing the query when data doesn't change much, and avoid query preparation/execution-path creation, because the database keeps them up to date on every update.
detail: Teacher reframed it as materialized views: they are pre-computed tables that must be refreshed explicitly (via triggers), not kept up to date automatically, and suit infrequently changing data.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we use database views, right? That is also a form of caching

statement: A materialized view stores the result of a query (e.g. a join of several tables plus computations) as a separate, pre-joined and pre-computed table; queries are then fired on the view instead of the base tables.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This view is already pre-joined, pre-computed, and it makes your things very fast.

statement: Materialized views are typically a property of relational databases, though some non-traditional databases also use them for performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is typically a property of relational databases, but there are some non traditional databases that also leverages this

statement: In relational databases one of the biggest performance concerns is joins: e.g. if ~80% of queries/load come from joining six tables and that data doesn't change frequently, store the joined result as a separate table (a materialized view).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say you're joining six different tables, almost for 80% of queries or 80% of load comes from those joining of six different tables.

statement: A materialized view can hold not just joins but other computation, such as added computed/derived columns.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: not just join, but let's say you want to add another column, a computed column, a derived column

statement: Example: raw table has marks for each subject in separate columns; a view adds a derived 'total' column and joins in other details of the people, and all queries run against that view.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have marks for each subject in a separate column and I want to have a total another column.

statement: Materialized views must be updated explicitly; database triggers are used to 'refresh' them (refresh is the official term).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to update explicitly, which is where database triggers come to the rescue.

statement: Materialized views give significant database performance gains only when data changes infrequently; with frequently changing data the frequent refreshes slow things down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But this works where your data changes infrequently.

statement: Materialized views are one of the most interesting database optimizations; many backend/API engineers don't understand them, while data engineers use them day in and day out (their bread and butter) to hyper-optimize analytical queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Materialized views are data engineers' bread and butter

statement: Read about DB views and materialized views and, most importantly, implement them: without implementation everything is theoretical.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Most importantly, implement, right? Without implementation everything is theoretical

statement: What a materialized view caches/saves is the expensive database computation, in particular the expensive join.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is saving that expensive database computation, that expensive join.

statement: A student suggested web browsers (caching in local storage to save network I/O) and CDN servers (like Netflix) as cache locations; the teacher took them one at a time.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: our web browsers. Basically, they save our network I.O. while by caching things, caching things in the local storage itself.

statement: The browser is a place where you can cache static images, static assets and even some API responses, so the client doesn't even need to call the backend server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This way you don't even have to make calls to your backend server to get some information

statement: A JWT token can be saved in the browser so a bunch of computation is saved.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For the JWT token, you may want to save it, so those, so you save bunch of computation.

statement: Web workers can do work offline and sync with the backend when the internet comes back; changes are made locally and pushed to the backend periodically, so the app feels very fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are web workers now that does everything offline, and then when internet comes back up, they sync back up to the back end

statement: Browser local storage is an excellent place to cache a bunch of stuff.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So browsers local storage is an excellent place to cache bunch of stuff.

statement: A student proposed fixing local-cache inconsistency with a cache that supports publish/subscribe, where all API servers publish and subscribe to updates. The teacher stopped the discussion so people new to these terms don't get confused and deferred it to next week.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Let me come back to this. Next week we'll be touching upon this.

statement: A student's team cached personalized recommendations (re-ranked products on category pages) client-side mainly for user perception, not latency: re-ranking on every revisit confuses users while never updating for a full day loses personalization, so they ran experiments to find the optimal cache duration, and accounted for the cache effect when preparing training datasets.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we did some experiments and found like optimal time of for how much time we have to store these recommendations

statement: Hypothetically, Amazon could store a user's recommendations in the browser's local storage on the device and render from there instead of making an expensive backend computation call, refreshing them periodically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I store it in my browser's local storage on my apps device. And you just use that to render it.
flags: check: "that's an excellent" at 00:24:15 may be teacher talking over student

statement: Hack: if you have 50 recommended items but the viewport shows only 10, pick 10 at random on each view; users feel recommendations are fast and fresh although they update only once a day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say you recommend 50 items, but on viewport, you can show only 10. So you pick 10 at random.

statement: A student's team cached at two levels: a Cloudflare CDN cached whole request responses, and Prerender.io cached JS files, CSS files and assets like images and videos.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We used to have CDN Cloudflare for caching the whole response of the request.

statement: Misconception: CDNs can only cache static things like images and videos. A CDN is just a proxy between you and the backend; to the CDN anything from the backend is just bytes, so it can cache literally anything, including API responses.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDNs are not just to cache images. Big misconception.

statement: API responses that are near-static (don't change often) can be cached on the CDN, so the request doesn't reach the backend or even the centralized cache; the CDN caches and distributes the response globally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So API responses that are near static can also be cached on the CDN.

statement: Search results for popular terms can be cached on the CDN; Giphy does this for its most popular terms.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: search results are popular terms. Right? Giphy uses that.

statement: Serving from the CDN saves your infrastructure from handling the request: normally users -> CDN -> backend -> database, but if the CDN has the answer the request never reaches your backend servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If your CDN itself has the answer, the request does not even have to come to your infrastructure.

statement: Example: an endpoint like https://search.abc.com/popular (all popular searches on the platform) can be cached on the CDN, which then serves it directly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can literally expose or cache HTTPS colon slash slash search.abc.com slash popular.

statement: CDNs are covered in depth in weeks 3-5, where they will be used in very interesting ways; today is only a sneak peek.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll go in depth of CDN in third week, fourth week, fifth week.

statement: A student proposed caching on the API server's disk as well as memory, to save the expensive network I/O call to the database or a cache; the teacher said this was exactly what he wanted to cover.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can also do this level caching, right? Because that would, that will save the expensive network IO call to the database or any cache.

statement: Don't think of a cache only as something that fits in memory: think of a cache as anything that helps you save an expensive computation or an expensive I/O.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Think of cache as anything that helps you save an expensive computation or an expensive IO.

statement: Every API server (EC2 instance, GCP VM) gets an attached disk (8 GB, 20 GB, ...) that holds only the OS, bundles, jar files and Python packages, so typically only 2-3 GB of a 20 GB disk is used; the rest is wasted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: out of those 20 GB, 2 GB, 3 GB are being used. They're not leveraging it enough.

statement: RAM caching is memory-bound and API server RAM is costly and scarce: of e.g. 8 GB, part goes to the OS, the application server and other jobs, leaving little room, while the 20 GB disk sits largely unused. So use the attached disk as a cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why not leverage the disk that is attached to the API server as a cache?

statement: A local disk read is much faster than the network I/O needed to read from a centralized cache; network is 'pathetically slow' compared to local disk reads, so a disk cache saves the expensive network call.
detail: Repeated at 00:31:41-00:32:38: few people use disk caching because they assume memory is fast, but the network I/O saved is what matters.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Disk is anyway faster than network IO.

statement: Cache on the API server's disk when inconsistency is acceptable, i.e. you don't need strong consistency between the servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So when inconsistency is okay, when you don't need strong consistency between them, are stateless, then you can actually cache some things on the disk

statement: During a similar discussion (in a past cohort), an engineer from Goldman Sachs got the idea of using the API server disk as a cache, applied it to optimize his system and it 'worked wonders'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that guy from Goldman Sachs, he got that idea, which did to optimize the system and worked wonders.

statement: Critically question every component of your infrastructure ('can I leverage this?'). If you take for granted that a cache is RAM-based and centralized, you will never come up with optimizations like disk caching.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you just take it for granted, if you just think cache is RAM based, cache is centralized, then you would never come up ...

statement: Very few people use disk as a cache because they assume memory is needed for performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: very few people use it. They think if I'm storing it on disk, how will I get this performance benefit?

statement: Always check whether caching gains you something: if the cached read is cheaper than whatever more expensive operation it replaces, it helps your system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whatever is more expensive than that, if you are saving it, you are helping your system thrive.

statement: Statutory warning for disk caching: there is no centralized view or consistency across servers, so a request to one server may return something different from another server. You must be okay with that; it is very use-case specific.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: statutory warning because given that you will not have consistency between this

statement: Load balancers and API gateways (e.g. nginx, AWS load balancer, API gateways) can also cache responses, like a CDN, so requests never reach the backend server, centralized cache or database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: load balancers like nginx, if you're using AWS load balancer, you are using API gateways, you are using there, you can cache the responses ...

statement: For every single component on the request route, ask: 'can I cache something here, and would it make my system better?' Depending on your architecture there will be different components, and each has a way to cache.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every single component in your request route is where you can ask this question that, hey, can I cache something over here?

statement: Cache levels along the common request path: local browser, CDN, load balancer / API gateway, API server RAM, API server disk, database (materialized views), and the centralized remote cache.
case_study: Applies to Medium's request path for serving blogs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So local browser, CDN, load balancer, API server RAM, API server disk, then database materialized views.

statement: Every cache is a trade-off (you gain some, you lose some). For local caches you trade strong consistency: if data changes infrequently, holding two copies doesn't matter, and if serving stale data for some time is okay, do it, it's 'the best thing ever'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But then you get some, you lose some. There is always a trade-off.

statement: Other students' caching ideas were deferred to the open forum at the end of class.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can add it at the end when we'll have open forum.
flags: check: name spellings (Sunay, Lanuba, Vikram, Amrit, Amrik, Harsh)

statement: The scaling section focuses on databases and how they are actually scaled in practice, not just the theory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk about databases part over here. And I'll tell you exactly how things are implemented.

statement: Scaling is the ability to handle a large number of concurrent requests. Concurrency is the key part: many requests in total are easy to handle, many at the same time are what make it challenging.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So scaling in general is having an ability to handle large number of concurrent requests. Now this concurrent is the key one.

statement: There are two typical scaling strategies: vertical and horizontal. Vertical scaling means adding more resources (RAM, CPU) to the same machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So vertical scaling is where you add more resources.

statement: Vertical scaling a database: 16 GB RAM -> 32 GB by changing the machine type in the AWS console, then 64, 128, 256, 512 GB, 1 TB, 2 TB, 4 TB. But you can't keep going beyond that; why?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You go to AWS console, change the machine type. The database is scaled up. 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1 TB, 2 TB, 4 TB.

statement: 'AWS doesn't give me an option beyond this' is the wrong (and weird) answer for why vertical scaling has a limit; the teacher heard it from a senior engineer. It is also not that large machines don't exist, since supercomputers do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot just say AWS does not give me an option, so I cannot do vertical scaling. That's the most weird answer that I ...

statement: A smartphone whose SD card slot supports 256 GB won't recognize a 512 GB card, because of a hardware limitation. The same applies to machines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What happens if I insert 512 in it? ... It would not recognize. Why it is not recognized? Because of hardware limitation.

statement: When two hardware components interface (USB stick in a port, network card or hard disk on the motherboard, RAM in its slot), data moves over buses (e.g. a USB stick's golden lines). Both sides must be compatible and speak the same hardware protocol (not HTTP) for sending bytes; if a component doesn't support a larger size, you cannot go higher.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These needs to be compatible with each other. They need to understand the protocol in which the data would be sent. Not HTTP protocol ...
flags: check: "MPT" course acronym as ASR wrote it
"cache lines" in "What happens is the cache lines that are there" may be misheard

statement: Vertical scaling cannot be infinite because it is limited by the capability of the physical hardware: going one level up needs literally different hardware, so unless the data center has that hardware you cannot go beyond. Software is an abstraction; at the end everything runs on physical hardware.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Vertical scaling is limited by the capability of the physical hardware on which things are running and not because of anything else.

statement: CS fundamentals (e.g. computer architecture, microprocessors) always go a very long way in system design reasoning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's always your CS fundamentals that goes a very long way.
flags: check: garbled sentence 'Computers has fundamentals always for the way.'

statement: The teacher spent his third year of college working in a data center, where his microprocessor professor answered his questions and demonstrated the physical limits behind vertical scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I spent my third year working in a data center because the professor loved me.

statement: Horizontal scaling means adding more machines: past the point where you can no longer vertically scale, one machine can't handle the traffic, so you spread it across multiple machines. It is generally preferred.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You want to add multiple machines, which is where horizontal scaling comes in.

statement: Linear amplification (a standard term): done right, horizontal scaling scales linearly. If one machine handles 100 requests/second and you need 500 requests/second, you need 500/100 = 5 machines.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you know that one machine can handle 100 requests per second, what if I want 500 requests per second? I would need 500 ...

statement: Amazon Prime Day: marketing/BI teams use prediction models to forecast orders; knowing the unit economics of one machine (requests/second a given configuration can handle), you compute machines needed = N / per-machine capacity to check whether you have enough infrastructure. This is critical for predictive scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the number of machines would be n divided by this. This is really critical when it comes to, when it comes to predictive scaling.

statement: Unit economics of a machine: the capacity (e.g. requests per second) that one machine of a given configuration can handle.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you know the unit economic of one machine, the unit tech economic of one machine.

statement: Autoscaling groups exist but don't work at scale: for large sudden spikes they fail miserably because they take their own sweet time to react.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Autoscaling groups exist, but they don't work at scale. If you want to handle large spikes, autoscaling groups fail miserably.

statement: A marketing campaign broadcasts a message (SMS, push notification) and users flood in as a sudden spike; the autoscaling group has no time to react before users arrive. So you prepare the infrastructure for the spike first and only then tell marketing to send the message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: before marketing team sends an SMS or a message or a push notification, you have to prepare your infrastructure to handle that spike.

statement: Massive marketing campaigns need coordination between teams (marketing must tell engineering beforehand); otherwise the infrastructure goes down, causing a massive outage, unhappy users and lost business. Scaling is a team game.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it doesn't happen, product is bound to fail. Infrastructure will go down.

statement: Autoscaling groups are fine for smaller spikes, where they have breathing space to scale up.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For smaller spikes like this and this and this, it's okay. Autoscaling group can handle.

statement: Load testing is the only way to know a machine's capacity (its unit economics). There is no magic formula; e.g. you cannot say a 32 GB machine handles 5000 requests/second without load-testing it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Load testing is the only way. No other way to do it but load testing.

statement: Vertical vs horizontal is not either/or; there is a sweet spot. A young product starts with vertical scaling, because horizontal scaling makes deployment complex, and scales horizontally after a certain stage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's not that you either vertically scale or there you horizontally scale. And so there's a sweet spot.

statement: Avoid premature optimization ('the root of all evil'): don't optimize infrastructure for unnecessary reasons; start simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But always ensure you don't do any premature optimization. That's the root of all evil.

statement: For Medium: start simple by vertically scaling the API servers, then put a load balancer in front and scale horizontally.
case_study: Medium's scaling path: vertical API servers first, then load balancer + horizontal API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We first vertically scale API servers and then put a load balancer and horizontally scale the system.

statement: Week 3 designs a load balancer and how it is implemented; for now it is drawn as a box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Third week we'll design a load balancer.

statement: Catch with horizontal scaling: people usually mean scaling API servers, but the extra requests the API servers accept are forwarded to their dependencies (database, centralized cache, other services), which go down if they aren't prepared for that scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just cannot scale things horizontally because when you add more machines ... what about the database?

statement: Always scale bottom-up: first ensure the database and other dependencies (other services) can handle the scale, scaling them explicitly for big campaigns, then horizontally scale the API servers, then let users in. For massive campaigns this is an org-level effort and dependent teams should document how they scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So whenever you are scaling, always do a bottom up scaling.

statement: Cascading failures, where one component going down takes down the components that depend on it until users can't use the platform, are the root cause of most major outages in distributed systems (the teacher says he has read many outage reports).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's always cascading failures that becomes the root cause of all, all the major outages.

statement: Before scaling up, make sure the components you depend on are scaled and can take the load; how they do it is their problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have to ensure that the components that you depend on, they are scaled, they're able to handle the load and then you scale up.

statement: The database is the most critical and most brittle component of the infrastructure: if the DB goes down everything is down, so scaling the database is the most basic thing to do.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: database is the most critical and the most brittle component of our infrastructure.

statement: The easy way to scale a database is vertical scaling (pick a bigger machine type in the AWS console); because vertical scaling has a limit, you then need horizontal scaling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You go to AWS console. A machine type, you get a bigger database

statement: In most applications the read:write ratio is about 90:10 or 99:1, heavily skewed toward reads.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the read to write ratio is 90 is to 10 or 99 is to 1

statement: Readers outnumber writers almost everywhere: many more people read a blog than create one, and on YouTube many more watch content than create it.
case_study: Medium is read-heavy: far more readers than writers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: even in blogging application, a lot of people would read the blog versus create the blog.

statement: Since most database traffic is reads, handling reads well largely solves the scaling problem, which is where read replicas come in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you handle reads well, problem is solved.

statement: Read replica setup: a master node and a replica node with asynchronous replication wired between them, almost a native database feature that you configure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is an asynchronous replication that is wired between the two and it's almost a native property of the database.

statement: Setting up replication is something SRE teams do day in and day out; if you don't know how, search e.g. 'how to set up MySQL replication'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just do a Google search, how to set up MySQL replication or any database replication.

statement: It's usually said that writes on the master are sent (pushed) to the replica. In reality the replica calls the master and pulls the changes; the master doesn't push. This is how asynchronous replication actually works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Master is not pushing the changes to the replica. Replica is pulling the changes from the master.

statement: All writes go to the master and are replicated asynchronously to the replica, and you want reads to go to the replica. The database doesn't route reads and writes automatically; you (the application) do the heavy lifting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database automatically does not do anything. You have to do the heavy lifting.

statement: Naive read/write split: in the API server code, create two connection strings and two database connection objects, one for the master and one for the replica, and in business logic pick the right one per query, e.g. reading a user's profile uses the replica connection and creating a blog uses the master connection.
case_study: Medium: profile reads via replica connection; blog creation via master connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There in the connection string, you pass two connection strings and you create two database objects.

statement: Tools and 'magic layers' exist that route automatically, but in the most basic implementation you decide, based on your use case, which reads are non-critical (replica) and which are critical (master).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are the one who can, who know, depending on your use case, which reads are not so critical and can be from replicas

statement: Banking: reading a user's profile can go to the replica, but reading the account balance is a critical read that must go to the master; otherwise a friend says the money was sent but you don't see it yet because of replication lag.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: reading of account balance have to go to master.

statement: This applies to MySQL, Postgres or MongoDB: create two connections, and in each API handler use the connection object that matches the use case to fire the query.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Remember connecting MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB. Create two connections.
flags: teacher said "which writes are not so critical that you can send to replica" here; context implies reads (not fixed)

statement: Intermediate proxy layers that do the read/write routing are covered in week 5 or 6; today only the basic implementation is shown.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There's an intermediate proxy layer. We'll talk about it in fifth or sixth [?week]

statement: When the master still gets more traffic than it can handle even after adding replicas and vertically scaling it, you shard the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now what happens when you get more traffic than that on your master? You vertically scale your master, but what happens beyond that? Which ...

statement: Sharding: when the data or load is so huge that one node can't handle it, split the data into mutually exclusive subsets and distribute them across multiple nodes (three in the diagram). All shards are masters, and each may have its own replicas.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you create three mutually exclusive subset of data and distribute it among the three nodes that you have. All the three are master.

statement: The API server holds the routing logic that decides which database to go to: e.g. shard by user ID using hash-based routing (hash of user ID), and the user-to-shard mapping must be fixed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So hash of user ID and you do hash based routing.

statement: Naive sharding: the API server opens a connection to every shard (3 shards = 3 database connections), determines which user each request is for, forwards it to that shard, gets the answer and returns it.
case_study: Medium can shard by user ID, with the API server routing to the right shard.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you have three shards or API server creates three database connections

statement: Implement naive sharding locally first. Production systems often put fancy proxy layers in between, but not all databases have them, so understanding the basic way is essential before adding that complexity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Highly recommend you to do this locally.

statement: Sharding proxy layers are covered in week 5; database concurrency and transactions are covered next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll talk about it in week five

statement: Scaling API servers is easy because they are stateless (autoscaling groups, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, load balancers); things get interesting when scaling data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: API servers are stateless. It makes your life very simple, but things become very interesting when you'd want to scale a data.

statement: The three common ways to scale a database: vertical scaling, read replicas, and sharding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These are three very common ways of scaling a database.
flags: the three ways are not enumerated at this timestamp; inferred from the section

statement: When the master goes down, leader election among replicas (a replica is promoted to master) is a way to recover from failures automatically, but you won't always see it in production. If you are building AWS you must implement it; if you use AWS, AWS does it internally and promotes a standby/replica to master for you.
detail: Student 1 asked about master failure and described a tree of replicas with synchronous propagation and voting/leader election.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: If you are building AWS, you would have to do leader election. But if you are using AWS, AWS itself will do leader election ...

statement: Implementing leader election yourself is a pain, and most product companies don't need it because the cloud gives those guarantees.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because implementing it is a pain and not product companies need that because cloud gives you those guarantees.

statement: Leader election is covered next-to-next week and comes up in three different places in the course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll talk about leader election at three different places.

statement: If you only ever pass a single connection string, the read/write routing is abstracted away by a proxy-like layer doing the heavy lifting. Not everyone has such a layer, so the naive way is for the API server to do it itself.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: you are providing one connection string and it is doing this heavy lifting for right. And not everyone would have that.

statement: Q: doesn't maintaining connection pools (and heartbeats) to multiple databases load the API server? A: you need it anyway; the API server must hold connections to all the databases to forward each request to the right one.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: But you need that, right? You need that

statement: Each database needs its own separate connection pool because TCP connections between a server and a database are stateful. Either the API server or a proxy can maintain the pools to the databases.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: you need to have a separate TCP connection pool for every one of them, for every database.

statement: Shards are not three identical copies of the database: each holds an exclusive subset, e.g. a third of the rows each.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: No, these are exclusive subset of data. So a third of rows will be over here.

statement: A student suggested putting different tables on different databases (e.g. 30 of 100 tables elsewhere); the teacher agreed this is vertical sharding, which also requires connection pools to each database.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if I have a hundred tables in my application, so we can have 30 tables somewhere. Correct. Vertical sharding

statement: Autoscaling EC2 instances is horizontal scaling: it adds more instances, e.g. a step-scaling rule like 'when average cluster CPU utilization goes above 60%, add one more node'.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: when an average CPU utilization of the cluster goes beyond 60%, add one more node.

statement: An autoscaling group (from AWS or any cloud) is only responsible for spinning up instances and adding them behind the load balancer. You must define the scale-up and scale-down rules yourself, e.g. based on average CPU utilization of the cluster.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Autoscaling group will just spin up instances and add it behind a load balancer. We have to define the rules
